summary: This unit teaches you to plan an electrical job from the first request to the handover. You will learn to find out exactly what is needed, break the job into steps, estimate time, people and materials, draw a bar chart, plan for safety (including safe isolation) and quality, and agree the plan with your supervisor and customer. You will also learn to keep the job on track, deal with problems and changes, finish and hand over properly, and review the job afterwards.

blocks.p: Every electrical job, from one outlet in a shop to the wiring of a new house, goes better when it is planned. A good plan makes sure the job is safe, that the right materials and tools are on site, that the work meets the drawing and the code, that it is finished on time and at the agreed price, and that the customer knows what is happening. This unit is for Level 2 trainees who plan their own small jobs and help their supervisors plan larger ones.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Find out what the job needs
Read the work order, drawings and specification, ask the customer and supervisor, and visit the site to measure and check.
List the tasks in a sensible order, see which must wait for others and which can run side by side.
Estimate each task, add an allowance for delays, and work out how many people and days are needed.
Show each task as a bar across a timeline, and use it to check progress.
Work out quantities from the drawing with an allowance for waste, check stock, order in time and check deliveries; list and check tools.
Carry out a risk assessment, choose controls in the right order, plan safe isolation, and know the emergency arrangements.
Find the standard the work must meet and plan checks at each stage, with the dead tests at the end.
Agree it with your supervisor, tell the customer about power-off times, brief the team and work around other trades.
Check progress against the plan, report problems early, and agree any change before you make it.
Clean up, sort waste, update the drawing and records, hand over to the customer and review what went well and what to improve.

flow: Find out what is needed
Plan: steps, time, materials, safety, quality
Agree the plan and prepare
Do the work and check it as you go
Finish, test and hand over
Review and learn for next time

blocks.note: In Jamaica a new or altered electrical installation must be inspected and certified by a licensed electrical inspector, under the Government Electrical Regulator (GER), before JPS will connect or reconnect it. A good plan allows time for this, and for any work the inspector asks to be put right.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a job from the first request to the review. Work through the examples with a calculator. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will show you the Centre's own planning forms.

sections.title: Finding out what the job needs

blocks.p: The first step in planning is to find out **exactly** what is wanted, where, to what standard and by when. A job planned on a guess is often done twice.

head: Source
What it tells you
rows: What job is to be done, where, for whom, by when, and the job number used on every record.
Where each light, switch, outlet, panel and cable route goes. The scale lets you measure lengths; the key explains the symbols.
The type and standard of materials and workmanship: cable type and size, conduit type, makes of fittings, mounting heights, finishes.
What is really wanted, any limits (opening hours, noise, power-off times), and answers to your questions.
How to fix, connect and use each product safely, and any limits such as weight or temperature.
**Electrical code and the Centre's or company's rules**
The safety standard the work must meet so that it is safe and passes inspection.
The real conditions: wall types, routes, obstacles, access, where the panel is and whether it has space.
**Earlier job records and the store's stock list**
What was installed before, what problems were met, and what materials are already in stock.

ul: What do you want, and what is it for? (A clipper outlet behind a counter needs a different height from a floor-level outlet.)
Exactly where do you want each item? Mark the positions on the drawing or on the wall with the customer.
When can the power be off, and for how long? What must stay on (fridges, computers, alarms, medical equipment)?
What hours may we work, and is there anything noisy or dusty we must avoid?
Where can we park, store materials and get water and toilets?
By what date must it be finished?
Measure rooms, heights and cable routes, and check them against the drawing.
Look at the panel: is there a spare way for a new breaker? Is the panel in good condition and labelled?
Check the walls and ceilings: block, concrete, wood or gypsum board; any beams, pipes or ducts in the way.
Look for hazards: work at height, old wiring, damp, overhead lines outside, other trades working nearby.
Check access for ladders and materials, and where the team can work safely.
Take photos and notes, with the date.

blocks.p: Electrical drawings are drawn to a **scale**. A scale of **1:50** means that 1 mm on the drawing stands for 50 mm in real life. To find a real length, measure on the drawing with a scale rule or ruler and multiply by the scale number.

ul: To change millimetres to metres, divide by 1,000.
The **key** (legend) explains what each symbol means: light, one-way switch, outlet, panel, and so on. Count each symbol to build the materials list.
The **title block** gives the drawing number, the scale, the date and the revision. Check you have the latest revision.
Written figures (dimensions) on the drawing are more reliable than measuring with a ruler. If a figure and a measurement disagree, ask.

blocks.note: Paper can stretch and copies can be enlarged or reduced. If a measured length looks wrong, check it against a written dimension or measure on site.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A **quotation** is a firm price given to the customer before the job: if they accept it, that is the price, unless the job changes.
An **estimate** is a careful guess at the cost, which may change.
The **deadline** is the date or time by which the job must be finished. Plan back from it.

blocks.p: A job is easier to plan, share out and check when it is broken into separate tasks. Then the tasks are put into the order in which they must be done, so that no work has to be undone or done twice.

blocks.h: Typical order for a new circuit in conduit

flow: Mark out the positions of boxes, fittings and routes
Fix the boxes and conduit
Pull in the cables
Fit and connect the lights, switches and outlets
Connect at the panel, with the supply isolated
Inspect and carry out the dead tests
Energise and carry out live checks (competent person)
Clean up, update records and hand over

ul: Some tasks **must wait** for another to finish: you cannot pull cables until the conduit is in, and you cannot test until everything is connected.
Some tasks **can run side by side** if there are enough people: one person can fit boxes in one room while another bends conduit for the next.
Some tasks can **start part-way**: cables can be pulled into the runs that are already finished while the last boxes are fixed.
Some steps are **hold points**: work stops until someone checks or approves it, for example an inspection before walls are closed or before the supply is connected.

head: Tool
What it is
What it is for
rows: The tasks written in order, with a time for each
Boxes for the steps joined by arrows, with diamonds for decisions
Showing the order and the choices, such as 'Test passed? Yes / No'
Each task drawn as a bar across a timeline
Showing when each task starts and finishes, and checking progress
Dates and times for each task and who does it
A list of items to tick off
Making sure no step, tool or check is forgotten
A written description of how a task will be done safely, step by step
Showing the team the safe method; often kept with the risk assessment
The company's fixed written method for a routine task
Making sure routine work, such as safe isolation, is always done the same safe way
A written approval, signed by an authorised person, for a high-risk task
Controlling dangerous work such as hot work, roof work or work in confined spaces

blocks.p: **A permit to work** states the task, the place, the hazards, the controls that must be in place, the time it is valid and who is doing the work. Work starts only when the permit is signed, and the permit is signed off when the work is finished and the area is safe.

blocks.note: Write each step so that someone else could follow it: start with a doing word ('Fix', 'Pull', 'Test') and say where ('Fix 20 mm conduit from panel to light box L1').
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Time, people and the bar chart

ul: Hours to minutes: multiply by 60. Minutes to hours: divide by 60.
To add times in different forms, change them all to minutes first, add, then change back. **Example:** 50 min + 1.5 h + 2 h 40 min = 50 + 90 + 160 = 300 min = **5 h**.
Be careful: 1.5 h is 1 h 30 min, not 1 h 50 min.
Use your own experience, your supervisor's advice and the times recorded on earlier jobs.
Think about the conditions: drilling concrete takes longer than gypsum board; high ceilings need ladders or a tower; an occupied building means working round people.
Include time to set up, collect materials, clean up and travel.

Add an **allowance for delays** (contingency) that you cannot foresee, such as a late delivery, a hidden obstacle or waiting for the power to be switched off. On small jobs many firms add about 10 to 20%, but follow your supervisor.

blocks.p: A **labour-hour** (or man-hour) is one person working for one hour. A task estimated at 12 labour-hours could be done by one person in 12 hours, or by three people in about 4 hours.

head: To find
Working
Example
rows: Time with a number of people
People needed to meet a deadline
Hours each person works ÷ hours worked per day

blocks.note: More people do not always mean less time. Some tasks need two people (pulling long cables, lifting a heavy fitting), and some cannot be split. Too many people in a small room get in each other's way.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: List the tasks down the left side in the order they will be done
Draw the time across the top: days, split into mornings and afternoons, or hours
Draw a bar for each task from when it starts to when it should finish
Start a task that depends on another only after that one ends
Mark key points, such as when the power must be off, a delivery, or an inspection
Add a title, the job number and the date

blocks.p: **Example: two people, a small office, 16 labour-hours (8 hours each), two days.** Each ■ is half a day.

blocks.h: Using the bar chart while you work

ul: At set times (for example at lunch and at the end of each day), shade each bar to show how much of that task is done.
Draw a line down the chart at today's time. A bar not shaded up to the line is **behind**; a bar shaded past it is **ahead**.
If the job is falling behind, tell your supervisor **early**, while there is still time to bring in help, change the order or tell the customer.
Never shade a bar for work that has not been done. The chart is only useful if it is honest.

blocks.p: Make a materials list so that everything needed is on site when work starts, and nothing is wasted by over-ordering. For each item give the **description, size or type, quantity and unit**, and say where it is coming from (store or supplier).

flow: Count each symbol on the drawing: lights, switches, outlets, boxes
Measure each conduit and cable route at the drawing's scale
Add the drops down to switches and outlets and the extra at each box and at the panel
Add an allowance for waste and off-cuts (often about 10%)
Round up to the units the supplier sells: whole lengths, rolls or boxes
Add fixings, saddles, couplers, connectors, labels and consumables
Check the store's stock, then order the rest in good time

blocks.p: **Example.** The conduit routes total 23.5 m. Adding 10% for waste: 23.5 × 1.1 = 25.85 m. PVC conduit is sold in 3 m lengths: 25.85 ÷ 3 = 8.6, so order **9 lengths**. Always round **up**: 8 lengths (24 m) would leave you short.

**Example.** A lighting run needs a line, a neutral, a switched line and a grounding conductor, each about 26 m including the extra at boxes. Each conductor colour comes from its own roll, so check that each roll has at least 26 m (plus waste) left, or order a new roll. A job that needs 230 m of one colour from 100 m rolls needs **3 rolls**.

blocks.note: In Jamaican hardware stores many electrical materials are sold in US units: conduit in 10 ft (about 3 m) lengths, building wire in rolls of 500 ft (about 152 m), and wire sizes in AWG. Check the unit before you order, and write it on the list.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Check each item against the **delivery note** and your order: the **type, size, quantity** and condition.
Report any shortage, damage or wrong item at once, and write it on the delivery note before you sign. Sign only for what actually arrived.
Do not use a wrong item 'to keep going': a smaller cable, a different conduit or an indoor fitting outdoors may not meet the specification or the code.
Store materials safely and securely, off wet ground and out of the sun where needed.

head: Item
Check before the job
rows: Right tools for the job; insulated tools undamaged; blades sharp.
Case, cable and plug undamaged; guards in place; inspection label in date.
Right type (fibreglass for electrical work) and height; no damage; book a tower in advance if needed.
Voltage tester and proving unit, continuity and insulation resistance testers: working, leads undamaged, calibration in date.
Locks, tags, PPE, barriers and signs, first-aid kit and fire extinguisher.

blocks.p: Any tool or ladder that is damaged is **labelled out of use and reported**, never taken to the job. Shared equipment, such as a scaffold tower, a cable drum stand or an insulation tester, may need to be booked: put it on the plan with the day it is needed.

A **hazard** is anything that could cause harm: a live conductor, a ladder, a drill, dust. A **risk** is how likely the harm is, and how bad it would be. Planning for safety means finding the hazards of every task before the job starts and deciding how to control them.

flow: Look at each step of the job and the place where it will be done
List the hazards
Decide who could be harmed (workers, customer, staff, public) and how
Judge the risk: how likely, and how bad
Choose controls, starting at the top of the hierarchy
Write it down and explain it to the team before work starts
Review it whenever the job or the conditions change

blocks.p: A simple risk matrix like this helps you decide which hazards need the most attention. High risks must be reduced before work starts.

head: Order
Control
Electrical example
rows: Isolate and prove dead, so there is no live work; fit surface trunking so that no wall has to be chased and no dust is made
A battery drill instead of a mains drill outdoors; a lighter ladder; a less dusty cutting method
GFCI protection, a vacuum attachment on a wall chaser, guard rails on a tower, a barrier round an open floor trap
Lock out and tag out, a permit to work, signs, a toolbox talk, training and supervision
Safety glasses, dust mask, gloves, safety boots, hard hat

blocks.p: Any work on an existing circuit must be planned so that it is done dead. The plan should say:

ul: **When** the power will be off and for how long, agreed with the customer.
**Which** breaker or isolator feeds the circuit, from the panel schedule, and how it will be confirmed.
**What equipment** is needed: a lockout device and personal padlock, a danger tag, a two-pole voltage tester and its proving unit.
**The procedure**: switch off, lock off, tag, prove the tester on the proving unit, test between every pair of conductors at the point of work, prove the tester again, then start.
**Other supplies** to isolate: a standby generator, solar PV, a UPS.
That the work will **never** be done live.

head: Hazard
Planned control
rows: Fibreglass ladder or tower of the right height, set up correctly; three points of contact; no over-reaching.
Drilling into hidden cables or pipes
Check drawings, use a detector, ask the owner, isolate nearby circuits if in doubt.
Dust from cutting block and concrete
Avoid chasing where possible; vacuum attachment or wet cutting; dust mask and glasses; clean up with a vacuum, not a broom.
Plan noisy work for times agreed with the customer; hearing protection.
Get help with drums and heavy fittings; lift with your legs, not your back.
Drinking water, shade and breaks; plan roof and outdoor work for the cooler part of the day.
Plan outdoor work for dry periods; GFCI protection; keep tools and leads dry.
Barriers and signs; keep walkways clear of tools and cables; never leave live parts or open boxes unattended.

ul: Where the **first-aid kit** is and who the trained first-aider is.
Where the **fire extinguishers** are: CO2 or dry powder for electrical fires, never water or foam.
The **evacuation plan**: the escape routes and the assembly point.
Emergency numbers in Jamaica: **110** for ambulance and fire, **119** for police, with the site's exact address and a landmark.
How to isolate the supply quickly in an emergency.

blocks.note: Hold a short **toolbox talk** at the start of each job, and each day on longer jobs: go over the day's tasks, who does what, the hazards and controls, the isolation arrangements and the emergency arrangements. Make sure everyone has understood, and let them ask questions.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A plan only works if everyone who is affected knows about it. Most problems on small jobs come from someone who was not told.

head: Who
What they need to know
Why
rows: The plan, the timing, any problem or change, and the results at the end
They are responsible for the job, approve the plan and can see problems you may miss
What will be done, when the power will be off, any noise or dust, any change and its cost
So they can plan their business or home around the work and there are no surprises
Their own tasks, the hazards and controls, the isolation arrangements and the finish time
So that everyone works safely and nothing is left undone or done twice
Where and when you will be working
So you do not damage each other's work or get in each other's way
The materials list and the date they are needed
So that items arrive on time
When the installation is ready for inspection and connection
So that the job can be certified and connected without delay

blocks.h: Sharing the work in a team

ul: Give each member **clear tasks** that match their skills, with a time to finish.
Make sure tasks that depend on each other are done in the right order.
Agree who is in charge of isolation and who holds the locks.
Check in with each other at set times, and help a member who is behind.
Listen to others' ideas; a trainee often spots a problem first.

blocks.p: Customers often ask for extra work part-way through: 'While you are here, can you add a light outside?' Never just do it. Tell your supervisor, who agrees the extra work, its price and its effect on the finish date with the customer **in writing** (often called a variation). Then update the plan, the materials list, the risk assessment and the drawing.

blocks.note: Keep messages clear and short, and write down anything important: a power-off time agreed by phone should be confirmed by message or on the job card. Written records protect you, the company and the customer.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Doing the work: progress, quality and problems

ul: Check the work done against the bar chart at set times every day.
Check that the materials and tools for the next tasks are on site, so that nobody waits.
If a task is taking longer, find out why and tell your supervisor early.
If you are waiting for something, move on to other tasks that do not depend on it.

blocks.p: Find the standard the work must meet from the **specification, the drawings, the makers' instructions and the electrical code**. Then plan **check points during the job**, so that faults are found and put right before they are covered up, not at the end.

head: Stage
What to check
rows: Positions and heights measured against the drawing; routes clear of pipes and other services
Level and plumb, secure, the right size and type, bends smooth, no sharp edges
Right size and type, right colours, no damage to insulation, enough length at each box
Terminals tight, no bare copper showing, conductors in the right terminals, grounding conductors connected
Visual inspection, then the dead tests, with results recorded

ol: **Continuity of the protective (grounding) conductors**: each grounding conductor is unbroken from the panel to every box, fitting and outlet.
**Insulation resistance**: between line and neutral, line and ground, and neutral and ground, with lamps removed and sensitive equipment disconnected; a high reading in megohms shows good insulation.
**Polarity**: every switch is in the line conductor, and lamp holders and outlets are connected the right way round.

blocks.p: These are done with the circuit isolated and proved dead. Only when they pass is the supply connected, and then any live tests and checks (such as testing a GFCI with its button and the inspector's tests) are done by a competent, authorised person. Record every result on the test sheet.

blocks.h: When things do not go to plan

head: Problem
What to do
rows: The panel has no spare way for the new circuit
Stop and report before ordering materials; the supervisor decides the solution (for example a larger panel or a sub-panel) and agrees it with the customer.
The route is blocked by a beam, column or water pipe
Stop; report it; agree a new route with the supervisor; update the drawing and materials list. Never cut through a structural member.
Do not use them; report and return them; move on to other tasks while the right ones come.
Re-order the tasks to do work that does not need it; tell the supervisor if the finish date is at risk.
Heavy rain on a day planned for outdoor work
Swap to indoor tasks; never work with mains tools in the rain.
The customer asks for extra work
Refer it to the supervisor; agree it in writing; then update the plan.
A tool or ladder is damaged
Take it out of use, tag and report it; get a replacement.
A new hazard is found (for example old roof sheets that may contain asbestos)
Stop work in that area, keep people away and report it; the risk assessment must be updated before work goes on.
Make the area safe, give first aid, call 110 if needed, and report it.

blocks.note: Do not change the plan on your own. Stop, think about the effect on **safety, quality, time and cost**, tell your supervisor and suggest a solution. Record the problem and what was agreed, so that it can be learned from at the review.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Making the work safe and complete

ul: Every cover, faceplate and lid is fitted; no live part can be touched.
All tests are done and recorded; any fault found has been put right and retested.
Locks and tags are removed only by the people who fitted them, when everyone is clear and the work is complete.

head: Waste
What to do with it
rows: Collect and return to the store for recycling, as the Centre or company directs.
Re-usable pieces to the store; the rest in the general waste.
Keep whole and apart from other waste: they contain mercury. Dispose of them as hazardous waste.
Vacuum and bag; never sweep dry dust into the air.

blocks.p: Never burn or bury waste, and never leave it for the customer. Return tools and spare materials to the store, and report any tool that was damaged.

ul: **As-built drawing**: mark every change on the drawing (an outlet moved, a different route) so that it shows the work as it was really installed. The next electrician depends on it.
**Job sheet**: work done, materials used, hours worked, problems met and how they were solved.
**Test record**: every test result, with the instrument used, the date and the tester's name.
**Reports**: any accident, near miss or damage, on the proper form.

flow: Walk the customer round the finished work
Show which breaker controls the new circuit and how to switch it off safely
Show how to test any GFCI with its button, and how often
Hand over the paperwork: test results, as-built drawing, makers' leaflets
Explain any part still waiting for inspection or connection
Ask the customer to sign the job card to say the work is complete

blocks.p: After the job, the team and supervisor look back at it. The aim is to learn, not to blame.

ul: What went well, and should be done the same way again?
What went wrong, and why?
How did the real time compare with the plan? **Percentage over-run = (actual − planned) ÷ planned × 100.** For example, planned 16 h, actual 18 h: 2 ÷ 16 × 100 = 12.5% over.
Were the materials right, or was there too much or too little?
What would we plan differently next time?

blocks.note: Write the lessons down and use them when you estimate the next job. A team that reviews every job gets better at planning; a team that does not makes the same mistakes again.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can list the sources of information for planning a job and say what each one tells me.
I can work out a real length from a drawing using its scale, and use the key.
I can carry out a site visit and say what to check.
I can break a job into tasks and put them in a sensible order, and see which depend on others.
I can describe a flow chart, a checklist, a method statement, an SOP and a permit to work.
I can add times given in different forms and change between hours and minutes.
I can estimate the time for each task and add an allowance for delays.
I can use labour-hours to work out time, people and days.
I can draw a bar chart and use it to check progress.
I can make a materials list from a drawing, add a waste allowance and round up to whole units.
I can check a delivery against the delivery note and my order.
I can carry out a risk assessment and choose controls in the order of the hierarchy.
I can plan safe isolation, including the power-off time and the equipment needed.
I can describe the emergency arrangements the plan must include.
I can say who must be told about the plan and why, and run a toolbox talk.
I can plan stage checks and the dead tests in the right order.
I can deal with a problem or a change without changing the plan on my own.
I can finish a job: make it safe, clean up, sort waste, update the drawing and records, and hand over.
I can review a job and work out a percentage over-run.

terms: A drawing marked up to show the work as it was really installed, with every change.
A chart that shows each task as a bar across a timeline.
A list of items or steps to tick off so that nothing is forgotten.
Extra time or money allowed in a plan for delays and problems that cannot be foreseen.
The date or time by which a job must be finished.
The paper that comes with a delivery, listing what has been sent.
A careful guess at the time or cost of a job, which may change.
A chart that shows the steps of a job as boxes joined by arrows.
The order for choosing controls: eliminate, substitute, engineering, administrative, PPE.
A point in a job where work stops until a check or approval is done.
The document that says what job is to be done, where and by when.
One person working for one hour.
A written, step-by-step description of how a task will be done safely.
A written approval, signed by an authorised person, for a high-risk task.
Personal protective equipment: the last line of defence.
A firm price given to a customer before a job.
How likely a hazard is to cause harm, and how bad the harm would be.
A written check of the hazards of a job, who could be harmed and how to control them; also called a job safety analysis (JSA).
The ratio between a length on a drawing and the real length, such as 1:50.
Standard operating procedure: a fixed written method for a routine task.
A document that sets out the type and standard of materials and work.
A short meeting at the start of a job or a day to go over the tasks and hazards.
A change to the agreed work, agreed in writing with its price and effect on time.

c1.title: A barber shop in Port Antonio
c1.text: Mr Desmond Wright owns a barber shop in Port Antonio, Portland. The job card asks for two new ceiling lights with one switch, and three new 110 V outlets along the back wall, on one new 20 A circuit from the shop's panel. The drawing is at a scale of 1:50 and shows the outlets 300 mm above the floor. Trainee Kemar is preparing the plan with his supervisor, Mr Barrington Lewis. On the site visit, Mr Wright says he would rather have the outlets just above the counter top, where the barbers plug in their clippers.

c2.title: Rewiring a church hall in Brown's Town
c2.text: Electrician Miss Kerry-Ann Thomas and trainee Javier are to rewire the lights in a church hall in Brown's Town, St Ann, starting on a Monday. Their task list is: A mark out (2 h), B fix conduit and boxes (10 h), C pull in cables (6 h), D fit lights and switches (5 h), E connect at the panel with the power off (2 h), F inspect and test (3 h), G clean up and hand over (2 h). Each of them works 6 hours a day on site. The choir practises in the hall every Wednesday at 6:00 p.m.

c3.title: Extra outlets in a Porus dental clinic
c3.text: Dr Campbell's dental clinic in Porus, Manchester, needs two extra 110 V outlets in the treatment room, taken from an existing outlet circuit. The clinic is open from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday to Friday. The fridge in the back office, where the clinic keeps its medicines, is on the same circuit. The walls are plastered block. Trainee Rochelle is writing the risk assessment and the work plan with her supervisor, Mr Paul Henry.

c4.title: Changes at a Morant Bay guest house
c4.text: A team is wiring four new rooms at a guest house in Morant Bay, St Thomas. On the second day the owner, Mrs Hyacinth Barnes, asks trainee Odane to add two lights on the outside veranda 'while you are here'. The same morning, the supplier delivers 14 AWG cable instead of the 12 AWG cable that the plan lists for the new 20 A outlet circuits.

c5.title: Finishing a hardware shop job in Yallahs
c5.text: Trainee Sasha-Gaye and electrician Mr Neville Ricketts have finished new lighting and outlets for a hardware shop in Yallahs, St Thomas. During the job one outlet behind the counter was moved 600 mm along the wall to clear a new shelf. The job was planned to take 20 hours and took 23. The waste left on site includes copper cable off-cuts, PVC conduit off-cuts, cardboard boxes and two old fluorescent tubes taken down from the ceiling.

questions.q: The conduit run along the back wall measures 132 mm on Kemar's drawing. How long is it in the shop?
questions.why: At 1:50, every 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm in real life: 132 × 50 = 6,600 mm, which is 6.6 m. A written dimension on the drawing, or a tape on site, is a good check.

questions.q: What should Kemar do about Mr Wright's wish to have the outlets above the counter?
o: Fit them above the counter, since the customer is paying
Fit them at 300 mm, since a drawing can never be changed
Ask Mr Lewis to agree the change and mark up the plan
Fit two high and one low so that everyone is satisfied
questions.why: A change to the drawing must be agreed by the supervisor with the customer before work starts, and then written on the plan and drawing. It may change the materials, the time and the price. Guessing, or ignoring the customer, both lead to work done twice.

questions.q: The conduit routes total 19 m. Kemar adds 10% for waste. Conduit comes in 3 m lengths. How many lengths should he order?
questions.why: 19 × 1.1 = 20.9 m, and 20.9 ÷ 3 = 6.97, so round up to 7 lengths (21 m). Six lengths would give only 18 m, less than the route itself. Always round up to whole lengths.

questions.q: On the site visit, Kemar finds there is no spare space in the shop's panel for the new breaker. What should he do?
o: Report it before ordering, so the plan can be changed
Join the new circuit onto the breaker for the shop lights
Take out the water heater breaker and use its space
Plan to leave the new circuit unconnected for now
questions.why: The panel decides how the circuit can be connected, so this must be solved before materials are ordered. The supervisor may need a larger panel or a sub-panel, which changes the cost and time and must be agreed with Mr Wright. Doubling up on a breaker or removing another circuit is unsafe.

questions.q: If Miss Thomas and Javier share all the work equally, about how many working days will the job take?
o: 1.25 days
5 days
2.5 days
15 days
questions.why: The tasks add up to 2 + 10 + 6 + 5 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 30 labour-hours. Shared by two people that is 15 hours each, and at 6 hours a day that is 2.5 days. The plan should allow three days, which also gives a little time for delays.

questions.q: Task E, which needs the power off, falls on Wednesday. How should the plan deal with it?
o: Do it after choir practice, working by torchlight
Agree the time with the church and finish well before 6 p.m.
Switch off without warning, since it only takes about two hours
Ask the choir to practise without lights that evening
questions.why: Power-off times are agreed with the customer in advance and placed where they cause least trouble. Planning task E for the morning or early afternoon gives time to finish, test and restore the lights before the choir arrives. Working by torchlight is unsafe.

questions.q: Which task can Javier usefully start while Miss Thomas fixes the last few boxes of task B?
o: Pull cables into the runs that are already finished
Inspect and test the whole lighting circuit (task F)
Connect the new circuit at the church's panel (task E)
Clean up the hall and hand over to the church (task G)
questions.why: Cable can be pulled into finished conduit runs while the last boxes go up, which saves time. Testing, connecting at the panel and handing over all depend on the wiring being complete, so they must wait.

questions.q: At the end of day 1, task B should be finished, but only half is done because the walls are harder to drill than expected. What should Miss Thomas do?
o: Plan to leave out some of the tests on the last day
Say nothing and work faster for the rest of the job
Shade the bar for task B so the chart looks on time
Tell her supervisor now and agree how to catch up
questions.why: Reporting a delay early gives time to bring in help, re-order the tasks or tell the church about a new finish date. Skipping tests puts safety at risk, and a bar chart shaded for work not done is useless.

questions.q: Cutting chases in the treatment room walls would make a lot of dust. Which control is highest in the hierarchy?
o: Rochelle wears a dust mask while she chases the walls
A vacuum attachment is fitted to the wall chaser
Surface trunking is fitted, so no wall is chased
A sign asks patients to keep out of the room
questions.why: Fitting surface trunking (if the clinic agrees) removes the dusty task altogether, which is elimination: the top of the hierarchy. The vacuum attachment is an engineering control, the sign is administrative and the mask is PPE, the last line of defence.

questions.q: When should the plan put the work on the existing outlet circuit?
o: After 4:00 p.m. or at a weekend, as agreed with Dr Campbell
At lunchtime, switching off for as short a time as possible
During opening hours, working live so the clinic is not disturbed
Whenever suits the team, switching off at the main switch
questions.why: The circuit must be worked on dead, and a clinic cannot have its power cut during treatment. Agreeing a time outside opening hours lets the circuit be isolated, locked off and proved dead without risk to patients or staff.

questions.q: The medicine fridge is on the circuit that will be switched off. What should the plan include?
o: Unplug the fridge without asking, since the work is short
Move the fridge onto one of the new outlets before starting
Leave this circuit live and work on a different one instead
Agree with the clinic how to keep the medicines cold
questions.why: Telling the customer what will be off, and for how long, lets them protect what matters, for example by keeping the fridge shut, checking its temperature or moving the medicines. The new outlets are on the same circuit, so they would be off too.

questions.q: Which set of items must Rochelle put on the tools list for safe isolation?
o: A non-contact detector and a roll of insulating tape
A lock, a tag, a voltage tester and its proving unit
Rubber gloves and a full set of insulated screwdrivers
A neon test screwdriver and a 'men at work' sign
questions.why: Safe isolation needs a lock and tag to secure the breaker off, and a two-pole voltage tester proved on its proving unit before and after testing. A non-contact detector or a neon screwdriver cannot prove a circuit dead.

questions.q: How should Odane answer Mrs Barnes's request for two veranda lights?
o: Fit them now with spare cable from the van, to please her
Refuse, because a plan can never be changed once agreed
Pass it to the supervisor to agree in writing first
Fit them after hours and collect the payment himself
questions.why: Extra work changes the materials, time, price and hazards of the job, so the supervisor must agree it with the customer in writing first. Doing it quietly, or pocketing the money, causes disputes and may leave unsafe or uninspected work.

questions.q: Why must the 14 AWG cable not be used on the 20 A outlet circuits?
o: It is too small for a 20 A breaker and could overheat
It is too thick to fit in the conduit with the others
14 AWG cable may only be used on 220 V circuits
Its insulation colours do not match the drawing
questions.why: The lower the AWG number, the thicker the wire. 14 AWG copper is normally protected at no more than 15 A, so on a 20 A breaker it could carry more current than is safe and overheat. Report the error and wait for the right cable, working on other tasks meanwhile.

questions.q: The veranda lights are agreed. Besides the price, what must now be updated?
o: Only the drawing, once the job is completely finished
Nothing else, as long as the supervisor has been told
Only the invoice that will be sent to Mrs Barnes
The risk assessment, materials list and bar chart
questions.why: Outdoor lights bring new hazards (a wet location, work at height) and need weatherproof fittings and GFCI protection, more materials and more time. The risk assessment, materials list and bar chart must all change, and the drawing is marked up too.

questions.q: What must be done about the outlet that was moved 600 mm?
o: Nothing, since the change was small and the owner knows
Mark it on the drawing so it shows what was installed
Throw the old drawing away and draw a new one next month
Write the new position on the wall above the outlet
questions.why: The as-built drawing must show the work as it was really installed. The next electrician, the inspector and the owner rely on it to find cables and outlets safely. Memory and notes on walls are lost; records last.

questions.q: Which item in the waste needs special handling because it contains a hazardous substance?
o: The cardboard boxes
The PVC conduit off-cuts
The old fluorescent tubes
The copper cable off-cuts
questions.why: Fluorescent tubes contain mercury. They are kept whole, apart from other waste, and disposed of as hazardous waste. Copper off-cuts go back to the store for recycling, and cardboard is recycled where possible.

questions.q: By what percentage did the job over-run its planned time?
questions.why: Over-run = (actual − planned) ÷ planned × 100 = (23 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 15%. Dividing by the actual time (23) gives the wrong answer of about 13%. The review should record why it took longer.

questions.q: Three tasks take 45 minutes, 1 hour 20 minutes and 2.25 hours. What is the total time?
o: 3 h 50 min
4 h 20 min
4 h 05 min
4 h 30 min
questions.why: Change everything to minutes: 45 + 80 + 135 = 260 minutes. 260 ÷ 60 = 4 remainder 20, so 4 h 20 min. Remember that 2.25 h is 2 h 15 min, not 2 h 25 min.

questions.q: Which of these is an administrative control?
o: A permit-to-work system for all roof work
Safety glasses worn when drilling overhead
A guard rail along the open edge of a roof
A battery drill used instead of a mains drill
questions.why: Administrative controls are safe systems of work, rules, signs and training, such as permits, lock out and tag out, and toolbox talks. The guard rail is an engineering control, the battery drill is substitution and the glasses are PPE.
